questions.question_text: A HIV carrier with ring-like lesions on MRI scan is most likely to have a diagnosis of:
questions.explanation: Cerebral toxoplasmosis commonly affects patients with advanced HIV immunodeficiency.  Toxoplasmosis with CNS involvement in patients who are immunocompromised can be  severe and debilitating, and the condition may be fatal. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)  scan shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions with extensive surrounding oedema in  supratentorial as well as the infratentorial region.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following tests would be best used for testing executive function?
questions.explanation: The Trail Making Test (TMT) has two parts and the times taken to complete each part are  used to measure central executive functioning.  In Part A, the participant must draw a line to connect consecutive numbers, 1 to 25. This tests visual screening, processing speed, attention. In Part B the participant connects numbers and letters in an alternating progressive sequence (i.e. connect A-1-B-2-C-3 and so on). This tests central executive processes oftask-set inhibition, cognitive flexibility, and the ability to maintain a response set. In order to measure central executive functioning, the difference in time taken to complete TMT-B and TMT-A (which has little executive input) is calculated.

questions.question_text: A doctor, during a clinical interview, tells a patient, "I think I now have a good idea of your financial situation; perhaps we should talk about your family problems now". Which technique is the doctor utilising?
questions.explanation: Transition is an interview technique used when moving from one to another topic. The correct answer is: Transition.

questions.question_text: What is the most common finding in a newly diagnosed patient with Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation: Unilateral resting tremor is the most common presenting feature in Parkinson's disease. The correct answer is: Unilateral resting tremor.

questions.question_text: A patient is suspected to have temporal lobe damage resulting from a vascular lesion. Which of the following visual signs may be elicited on perimetry?
questions.explanation: Temporal lesions produce upper quadrantanopia due to damage to optic radiation. The correct answer is: Upper quadrantanopia.

questions.question_text: A patient breaks down and cries during interview. Which of the following technique is useful at this stage?

options.text: Ask a question with multiple choices

questions.explanation: Validation statements facilitate the continuation of a clinical interview by 'normalising' experiences. The correct answer is: Validation.

questions.question_text: Mr. Y has a diagnosis of chronic schizophrenia. He has polyuria, polydipsia and becomes acutely confused. On further investigation, his serum sodium levels are notably low. What do you suspect?
questions.explanation: Water intoxication occurs particularly in patients with chronic schizophrenia. The correct answer is: Water intoxication.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a feature of late-onset schizophrenia?

options.text: Family history of schizophrenia is infrequent when compared to early onset
White matter hyperintensities on MRI brain

correct_answer.text: White matter hyperintensities on MRI brain

correct_answers.text: White matter hyperintensities on MRI brain

questions.explanation: White matter hyperintensities are not associated with late-onset schizophrenia. The correct answer is: White matter hyperintensities on MRI brain.

questions.question_text: A 44-year-old man with schizophrenia has intense suspiciousness and persecutory delusions. He tells you that his neighbours want him to prepare a home-made explosive with detonators. Which of the following would be the best response at this point of interview?

options.text: Perhaps we should ask your neighbours if this is true
Why do you think your neighbours want you to do that?
No, I don't think this sort of thing could happen
If you prepare explosives, we may have to involve the police
It doesn't sound like a good idea to prepare explosives

correct_answer.text: Why do you think your neighbours want you to do that?

correct_answers.text: Why do you think your neighbours want you to do that?

questions.explanation: Asking why helps to collect clinically useful information while maintaining a good therapeutic relationship. The correct answer is: Why do you think your neighbours want you to do that?

questions.question_text: Obsessions can also occur as
questions.explanation: Obsessions often manifest as intrusive, unwanted thoughts, impulses or 'mental images'. The correct answer is: Mental images.

questions.question_text: A 67-year-old male admitted to A and E, when asked what the month was, replied 'January' and when asked what the year was, replied 'January' again. He is exhibiting
questions.explanation: Perseveration refers to repeatedly same response irrespective of changes in stimuli. The correct answer is: Perseveration.

questions.question_text: A patient with schizophrenia often rocks back and forth. He is also observed to be thumping his head with his fist for no apparent reason. He is exhibiting which of the following symptoms?
questions.explanation: This patient is demonstrating stereotypy; a symptom characterised by repetitive, functionless  motor behaviour.   Stereotypies, mannerisms, and verbigeration are often elicited in patients with catatonic  schizophrenia.   Hemiballism – hyperkinetic movement disorder characterised by violent involuntary proximal  limb movements on one side of the body, caused by damage to the subthalamic nucleus of  the basal ganglia. Unrelated to schizophrenia.  Ambitendency – a motor symptom where a patient who has been given an instruction  alternates between automatic obedience and negativism e.g. when asked to shake hands,  the patient appears indecisive, repeatedly extending and withdrawing their hand.  Ambivalence - described by Bleuler as one of the four primary symptoms of  schizophrenia and was defined as having positive and negative emotions at the same time.  Patients exhibiting ambivalence often have an inability to decide on an action.  Mannerisms - repetitive, goal-directed movements (e.g. saluting).

questions.question_text: A patient that you see in your hospital corridor is moving his closed fist round to the right and round to the left in a repetitive manner. He is exhibiting:
questions.explanation: Repetitive, non-goal-directed motor activity is called stereotypy. The correct answer is: Stereotypy.

questions.question_text: A man using mescaline 'smelt the noise of the trumpet'. This condition is known as:
questions.explanation: This is a classical example of synaesthesia described by Sims. The phenomenon of  perceiving a stimulus of one modality in a different modality (may be single or multiple  modalities) is called synaesthesia. E.g. tasting the music, hearing colours and smelling  voices. It is not a hallucination as the perceived object has an appropriate stimulus.  Reflex hallucinations are a hallucinatory form of synaesthesia. A stimulus in one modality  produces a hallucination in another modality

questions.question_text: A psychologist asked Mr. Snowden whether he had any special powers or abilities that other people do not have. He replied that he wasn't sure as he never visited Russia. When asked to clarify, he asked, "If you throw twenty-and-two blackbirds, would you know where does the evening start?" This form of speech is called:
questions.explanation: Tangentiality - speech is organised, but not goal directed. The subject answers a question in  an indirect manner with vague relevance. The answer appears distant and drifted away from  the original goal.

questions.question_text: In psychopathology, the term 'moria' refers to:

options.text: Tendency to choke when drinking fluids
Tendency to be restless and hyperactive

questions.explanation: Puerile, childish, frivolous, or silly behaviour occurs with right frontotemporal lesions and in  frontotemporal dementia. In such cases, moria (foolish or silly euphoria) and Witzelsucht (a  tendency to tell inappropriate jokes are seen).

questions.question_text: All are true regarding compulsions except

options.text: Compulsive acts often provoke further anxiety
They are always preceded by an obsessive thought
Washing is the most frequent compulsion
Can be an unobservable mental act

correct_answer.text: They are always preceded by an obsessive thought

correct_answers.text: They are always preceded by an obsessive thought

questions.explanation: Compulsions need not be always preceded by obsessive thoughts; they can be preceded by  obsessive images, words or impulses. In some cases of autism, Asperger's syndrome or  frontotemporal dementia, compulsive behaviours are noted without any preceding  obsessions.

questions.question_text: A man complains of repeated thoughts about self-harm. Which of the following is characteristic of obsessions?

options.text: These thoughts can be stopped at will

questions.explanation: Obsessions are recurrent and characterized by a stereotyped pattern, happening without much change. The correct answer is: They have a stereotyped pattern.

questions.question_text: While examining the mental state of a 47-year-old man with psychosis, you noticed a sudden stop in the flow of his thoughts. This phenomenon can be termed as
questions.explanation: Thought block is a symptom of schizophrenic thought disorder where the patient experiences a sudden break in thought flow. The correct answer is: Thought block.

questions.question_text: A 35 year old lady in your inpatient unit covers her head with a veil. She claims that other people can hear what she thinks. The most likely description is
questions.explanation: This lady is experiencing an intrusion into the privacy of her thoughts and others come know them 'as she is thinking'. Thought broadcast is generally described as a unique  phenomenon where, in a fashion similar to the live (radio or television) telecast of events,  one's thoughts appear to get diffuse or broadcasted to others. Another school of thought  suggests using this term when patients believe others can hear their thoughts as a  consequence of the thought echo phenomenon (where patients themselves can hear their  own thoughts). Pawar A and Spence S. Defining Thought Broadcast.The British Journal of  Psychiatry (2003) 183: 287-291

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a characteristic sign in a catatonic patient?
questions.explanation: Characteristic signs of catatonia include posturing, rigidity, echolalia, and mutism, but not typically tremors. The correct answer is: Tremors.

questions.question_text: A senseless repetition of words is known as
questions.explanation: Verbigeration refers to senseless repetition of sounds, words, or phrases. The correct answer is: Verbigeration.

questions.question_text: The most common modality of illusions is
questions.explanation: The most common modality of illusions is visual; they are not necessarily indicative of any psychopathology. The correct answer is: Visual.

questions.question_text: The concept of autochthonus idea was formulated by:
questions.explanation: Wernicke described autochthonous ideas as spontaneous or indigenous thoughts. The correct answer is: Wernicke.

questions.question_text: What defense mechanisms are commonly employed by patients with borderline personality disorder?
questions.explanation: Functionally, patients with borderline personality disorder distort their relationships by  considering each person to be either all good or all bad. They see people as either nurturing  attachment figures or as hateful, sadistic figures who deprive them of security needs and  threaten them with abandonment whenever they feel dependent. As a result of this splitting,  the good person is idealised and the bad person devalued.  Projective identification is another defense mechanism that often occurs in patients with  borderline personality disorder. In this primitive defense mechanism, the patient projects  intolerable aspects of themselves onto another person, inducing them to play the projected  role, and the two persons act in unison.

questions.question_text: A 34-year-old man who has a significant conflict with his partner has the following thoughts in the unconscious and the conscious level. I hate him (unconscious); I love him (conscious). This refers to which of the following defense mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Reaction formation involves expressing overt attitudes that oppose one’s unacceptable internal impulses. The correct answer is: Reaction formation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following can be considered as a neurotic defence mechanism?
questions.explanation: Reaction formation is considered a neurotic defense mechanism. The correct answer is: Reaction formation.

questions.question_text: You arrived late to a psychotherapy meeting and the therapist talks about 'Loss of ego boundaries'. Which of the following condition is she most likely referring to?
questions.explanation: Patients with schizophrenia often experience their ‘self’ as disembodied, and they feel empty,  unreal, dead, and differentiated from the world. They are unable to sustain a sense of self as  persons, which is why they are equally unable to experience neither separateness from nor  relatedness to others in a usual way. They may fear losing their identity in a relationship as  well as feel dependent on the other for their very being. The capacity for reality testing and  the relative intact ego boundaries in patients with borderline personality organisation are what  delimit these patients from the psychoses.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a mature defence mechanism?
questions.explanation: Sublimation is classified as a mature defense mechanism. The correct answer is: Sublimation.

questions.question_text: The term 'Dream Work' described by Sigmund Freud involves

options.text: Multiple images in dreams represent one unconscious impulse
Transforming latent content into manifest content
Transfer of energy from an original object to a symbolic representation of the object
Several unconscious impulses are combined into a single image

correct_answer.text: Transforming latent content into manifest content

correct_answers.text: Transforming latent content into manifest content

questions.explanation: Freud distinguished two types/layers of dream content. Manifest Content refers to what is  recalled by the dreamer; Latent Content refers to unconscious thoughts and wishes that  threaten to awaken the dreamer. The unconscious mental operation by which the Latent  Content is transformed into Manifest Content is called the Dream Work.

questions.question_text: There is no processing involved in which of the following types of memory?
questions.explanation: Sensory memory: This is modality specific, has a large capacity but gets disrupted by an  inflow of new information in the same modality.   Each sense has its own sensory memory e.g. iconic (visual), echoic (auditory). Iconic lasts for  0.5 seconds while echoic lasts for 2 seconds.   No processing is involved in sensory memory. Information that is attended to is transferred to  short-term memory store, and information that is not selected for processing is rapidly lost.

questions.question_text: All are examples of secondary drive except
questions.explanation: Drives refer to purposeful activity initially produced to satisfy an internal need. Drives are  commonly divided into primary and secondary drives.   Examples of primary drives are eating, drinking, sex.   Examples of secondary drives are affection, comfort, achievement, dominance and  socialisation. The secondary drives acquire their values through their association with primary  drives and often through a social learning process.

questions.question_text: A child received generous praise from her parents every time when she wrote a letter of the alphabet. She was praised more when she managed to write a full word. She was rewarded more generously when she wrote a sentence. Which of the following reinforcement is taking place?
questions.explanation: Shaping is an operant conditioning method for producing an entirely new behaviour by using  rewards to guide an organism toward a desired behaviour (called 'successive  approximations'). The organism is rewarded with each small advancement in the right  direction.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is one of the maladaptive traits that can be used to further describe a diagnosis of personality disorder in ICD-11?
questions.explanation: The maladaptive traits that can be used to describe a diagnosis of personality disorder in  ICD-11 are: negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition and anankastia.  A  further qualifier of 'borderline pattern' can also be used

questions.question_text: Lucy is learning to write. Her father praises her for holding the pencil correctly, then for scribbling something on a piece of paper and writing something vaguely which resembles like a letter. The learning theory principle employed here is:
questions.explanation: Shaping is a teaching technique that rewards successful approximations of a target skill to facilitate learning. The correct answer is: Shaping.

questions.question_text: Which of the following concepts is reflective of a change in ICD-11 (from ICD-10)?

options.text: Use of dimensional approach for all disorders
Removal of minimum symptom count for all disorders
Introduction of gender incongruence as mental health disorder
All disorders can be diagnosed at any age

correct_answer.text: All disorders can be diagnosed at any age

correct_answers.text: All disorders can be diagnosed at any age

questions.explanation: ICD-11 takes a lifespan approach to diagnosis, permitting diagnoses which were usually  associated with childhood or adolescence, such as attachment or conduct disorder, to be  diagnosed at any age.  It specifically considers the cultural background of a patient in  diagnosis.  A dimensional approach has been taken in personality and primary psychotic  disorders, as well as for depressive episodes in mood disorders.  Minimum symptom counts  have been removed from diagnostic criteria for most disorders, but not major  depression.  Gender incongruence, replacing gender identity disorder, has been moved to  the sexual health chapter of ICD-11 as it is not a mental health disorder.

questions.question_text: Who proposed the two-factor theory of intelligence?
questions.explanation: The two-factor theory of intelligence was postulated by Spearman. Spearman carried out a  factor analysis of the result of children's performance on a number of tests and concluded  that all tests measured both a common factor of general intelligence (g) and a specific factor  (s). He believed that individual differences were due to differences in (g).   According to Sternberg, component intelligence is used for executive tasks and experiential  intelligence is used for routine tasks that have already been learnt or mastered.

questions.question_text: A 44-year-old woman is terrified of heights. She develops a sense of vertigo even at 1st or 2nd floor of a building and avoids high rise buildings at all cost. The company she is working for undergoes relocation and she is required now to work at 15th floor of a building in central London. Which of the following is the best treatment option for her?
questions.explanation: Simple phobias such as acrophobia can be treated with the behavioural technique of  systematic desensitisation. Systematic desensitisation is based on the behavioural principle  of reciprocal inhibition (i.e. anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist). It involves three steps:  relaxation training, constructing a hierarchy of anxieties, and desensitisation of the stimulus.  The patient is exposed to a graded hierarchy of anxiety-provoking situations in stepwise  fashion while being taught to practice the relaxation techniques (e.g. a young woman with a  spider phobia is taught relaxation techniques and then exposed to experiences starting from  the lowest level of her hierarchy of anxieties - such as going to the cellar where there is the  potential to come across a spider - then progressively going up the ladder to the highest   such as handling a spider).

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man who works for the state as a highway and bridge designer becomes extremely anxious when he has to drive across any bridge. Which technique can best help him?
questions.explanation: Simple phobias such as acrophobia can be treated with the behavioural technique of  systematic desensitisation. Systematic desensitisation is based on the behavioural principle  of reciprocal inhibition (i.e. anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist). It involves three steps:  relaxation training, constructing a hierarchy of anxieties, and desensitisation of the stimulus.  The patient is exposed to a graded hierarchy of anxiety-provoking situations in stepwise  fashion while being taught to practice the relaxation techniques (e.g. a young woman with a  spider phobia is taught relaxation techniques and then exposed to experiences starting from  the lowest level of her hierarchy of anxieties - such as going to the cellar where there is the  potential to come across a spider - then progressively going up the ladder to the highest   such as handling a spider).

questions.question_text: A psychiatrist shows several pictures to encourage her patient to narrate imaginative stories and descriptions. On the basis of the responses, she makes an assessment of the patient's personality. Which of the following best describes this test?
questions.explanation: The thematic apperception test is a projective personality test. It consists of a series of 10  black-and-white pictures that depict individuals of both sexes and of different age groups,  who are involved in a variety of different activities. The stories that the patient makes up  concerning the pictures, according to the projective hypothesis, reflect the patient’s own  needs, thoughts, feelings, stresses, wishes, desires, and views of the future.

questions.question_text: According to Eysenck's three-factor theory which of the following is a feature of an extraverted person?

options.text: They have a less reactive reticular activating system
They have an overactive reticular activating system
They have a high autonomic lability

correct_answer.text: They have a less reactive reticular activating system

correct_answers.text: They have a less reactive reticular activating system

questions.explanation: Eysenck believed that differences in extraversion were due to physiological differences in  brain systems that caused some people to be more easily aroused than others. Specifically,  he proposed that the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) regulated arousal. People  differ in the sensitivity of this system, which causes them to respond differently to their  environment. A moderately stimulating environment might cause people with a very sensitive  ARAS to feel overstimulated and retreat (i.e., to behave like introverts), but people with a less  sensitive ARAS to feel under-stimulated and seek out additional stimulation (i.e., to behave  like extraverts).

questions.question_text: Recalling an address with three items tests which one of the following?
questions.explanation: Verbal memory involves the recall of verbal information such as words and addresses. The correct answer is: Verbal memory.

questions.question_text: A 39-year-old man can be tested for current IQ using
questions.explanation: The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) is designed for individuals aged 16 and over to assess general cognitive ability. The correct answer is: WAIS-R.

questions.question_text: Which of the following determines one's cultural identity?
questions.explanation: Race is perceived as a permanent entity determined by genetic ancestry and characterised  by physical appearance.   Culture is perceived as a changeable entity determined by upbringing and choice and  characterised by behaviours and attitudes.   Ethnicity is perceived as partially changeable entity determined by social pressure and  psychological need characterised by a sense of group identity and belonging.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a new mental health disorder under ICD-11?
questions.explanation: Prolonged grief disorder is recognized in ICD-11 as a persistent and disabling grief reaction lasting longer than 6 months. The correct answer is: Prolonged grief disorder.

questions.question_text: William Tuke's approach to the treatment of insanity was called
questions.explanation: William Tuke was a 19 century reformist and philanthropist notable for his work in mental  health. He was known for his strict self-discipline and judicious manner and was a firm  believer in the Quaker faith. Possibly catalysed by the very public mismanagement of King  George III’s ‘madness’, he pioneered the use of moral treatment, a humane method of  treating mental illness. This focused on allowing patients to live in a community, partake in  daily activities, and not be subjected to the brutality of the commonplace asylum. Tuke went  on to aid in the reform of the law with regards to asylums.

questions.question_text: The term stigma was first popularised by
questions.explanation: Stigma is a mark of disgrace associated with a person, a personal quality, or a personal  circumstance. In ancient Greece, bodily signs were sometimes cut or burnt into the bodies of  people to advertise their status as slaves, criminal, or traitors and to indicate that they were  blemished, ritually polluted, and to be avoided, especially in public places. The term was  introduced into the social sciences by sociologist Erving Goffman in a book entitled Stigma:  Notes on the Management of Spoiled Identity.

questions.question_text: A psychosomatic family process has been described in association with eating disorders. The features of such a psychosomatic family includes
questions.explanation: Minuchin and colleagues defined predominant characteristics of families with an anorectic  adolescent (so-called ‘psychosomatic families’), including enmeshment, rigidity, insufficient  conflict resolution skills, and overprotectiveness.

questions.question_text: Select the correct statement regarding schizophrenia in African-Caribbean population

options.text: Second generation African-Caribbeans with schizophrenia are more likely to develop negative symptoms
An increased rate of schizophrenia is not found in Jamaica, the country of origin for most African-Caribbeans in the UK.
The rate of prescription of depot medications for second generation African-Caribbeans in the UK are the same as that of Caucasian subjects
Second generation African-Caribbeans with Schizophrenia are more likely to have a continuous unremitting illness
The first admission rates for second generation African-Caribbeans in the UK are the same as that of Caucasian subjects

correct_answer.text: An increased rate of schizophrenia is not found in Jamaica, the country of origin for most African-Caribbeans in the UK.

correct_answers.text: An increased rate of schizophrenia is not found in Jamaica, the country of origin for most African-Caribbeans in the UK.

questions.explanation: First and second generation Afro- Caribbean migrants to the UK have increased rates of  psychotic illnesses (Mallett et al., 2002; Fearon et al., 2006; Selten et al., 2007). They are  more likely to receive depot antipsychotics, and are less likely to be prescribed second  generation antipsychotics. The rates of schizophrenia in Caribbean countries are no higher  than the incidence rates for the native White people in Britain, suggesting that genetic  predisposition alone cannot account for the high reported rates of schizophrenia in African  Caribbeans in the UK. In general, apart from the cultural influence on the content of  delusions, the psychopathological features of schizophrenia do not differ notably among  various patient groups.

questions.question_text: In developmental psychology, the term symbiosis refers to which of the following phenomena?

options.text: The dual entity of father and mother
The dual entity of mother and caregiver
The dual entity of mother and the infant
The dual entity of twin siblings
The dual entity of brother and sister

correct_answer.text: The dual entity of mother and the infant

correct_answers.text: The dual entity of mother and the infant

questions.explanation: Margaret Mahler proposed a theory to describe how young children acquire a sense of  identity separate from that of their mothers’. During symbiosis (age 2-5 months), mother  infant is perceived as a single fused entity.

questions.question_text: The mother of an autistic child wants to know why her son lacks empathy for other children. Which of the following concepts might best explain the fundamental defect?
questions.explanation: Theory of mind refers to understanding one's own and others' mental states, which is often impaired in autism. The correct answer is: Theory Of Mind.

questions.question_text: When a mother leaves an infant, the infant can become upset. To compensate and comfort for this sense of loss, an object with the attributes of the mother is required. Winnicott called this object
questions.explanation: Winnicott coined the term transitional object for items that serve as a surrogate for the mother, aiding in separation anxiety. The correct answer is: Transitional objects.

questions.question_text: From the matching items, identify the incorrectly matched correspondence between mother's AAI (Adult attachment interview) category and infant's SSP behaviour pattern (strange situation procedure).
questions.explanation: There is an 80% correspondence between a mother's attachment category on the AAI and  her infant's attachment pattern. This indicates that a mother's care-giving behaviour towards  her child is significantly influenced by her own attachment experience.   Studies have shown that mothers in the dismissing adult attachment category typically have  children who exhibit an avoidant attachment pattern, mothers in the pre-occupied/ entangled  adult attachment category typically have children who exhibit a resistant attachment pattern,  and mothers with unresolved attachment tend to have children with disorganised or  disorientated attachment pattern.

questions.question_text: Which of the following descriptions is suggestive of dissocial personality disorder?
questions.explanation: Dissocial personality disorder is characterized by a callous disregard for others and often has a background of childhood conduct disorders. The correct answer is: Evidence of childhood conduct disorder.

questions.question_text: ICD-10 diagnostic criteria for dissocial personality disorder includes:
questions.explanation: ICD-10 diagnostic criteria include:  a callous lack of concern for the feelings of others  an incapacity to maintain (not establish) enduring relationships  an incapacity to experience guilt  a persistent proneness to blame others  disregard for social norms  a very low frustration tolerance   Conduct disorder during childhood and adolescence, though not invariably present, may  further support the diagnosis.  Persistent irritability may be an associated feature

questions.question_text: Regarding 'Quality Of Life-16', which of the following is true:

options.text: It cannot be used in patients with chronic illnesses

questions.explanation: Flanagan's QOLS originally had 15 items, but was expanded to include a 16th item It measures five conceptual domains of quality of life:   1. material and physical well-being  2. relationships with other people  3. social, community and civic activities  4. personal development and fulfilment  5. recreation  It is most often used in samples with chronic illnesses. The QOLS is usually self  administered. It can also be completed by interview format. The QOLS can be completed in  about 5 minutes. Scores can range from 16 to 112.   Ref: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC26

questions.question_text: Charles Bonnet syndrome is associated with
questions.explanation: Charles Bonnet syndrome: Elderly patients, with normal consciousness and no brain  pathology, with reduced visual acuity due to ocular problems, experience vivid, distinct,  usually well-coloured (in contrast to real sensation that is blurred due to eye disease) formed  hallucinations – mostly humans, at times animals and cartoons. These objects usually show  movement, and can be voluntarily controlled – disappear on closing the eyes; insight about  unreality is usually preserved – though they may evoke emotions including fear and joy.  About 1/3rd are elementary; usually the hallucinations are located in external space

questions.question_text: Paramnesia is associated with
questions.explanation: Reduplicative paramnesia involves the belief that people or places have been duplicated, linked to Capgras syndrome. The correct answer is: Capgras delusion.

questions.question_text: Iconic memory lasts for
questions.explanation: Iconic memory holds stimuli for up to a second. As a consequence, the flow of visual  information seems smooth and continuous. The memory traces of auditory stimuli can last for  several seconds, many times longer than the traces of visual stimuli. Iconic memory (or iconic  store) is one of the sensory registers, allowing a visual image to persist for about half a  second (depending on brightness) after a stimulus has ceased. It enables television, which  presents 25 still images per second, each given twice to raise the flicker rate to 50 per  second, to convey the illusion of a single continuous image which can be perceived as a  moving image.

questions.question_text: A forensic investigator tries to reconstruct the crime scene and encourages the witnesses to visit the scene of crime to aid this process. Which recall phenomenon is being utilized by this investigator?
questions.explanation: Context dependent memory suggests that recall is improved when individuals are in the same context where they learned the information. The correct answer is: Context dependent memory.

questions.question_text: John loves to gamble using slot machines in the casinos. The reinforcement achieved using slot machines is a type of
questions.explanation: In operant conditioning, variable-ratio schedules provide reinforcement after a random number of responses, such as playing slot machines, which leads to high rates of behavior. The correct answer is: Variable ratio schedule.

questions.question_text: The Thematic Apperception Test is a projective test of
questions.explanation: The Thematic Apperception Test assesses personality by analyzing responses to ambiguous pictures, reflecting the individual's needs, feelings, and thoughts. The correct answer is: Personality.

questions.question_text: A gentleman gets his paycheck on the first day of every month. His salary provides which one of the following types of reinforcement?
questions.explanation: A fixed-interval schedule is when behaviour is rewarded after a set amount of time. This type  of schedule exists in payment systems when someone is paid hourly, weekly or monthly: no  matter how much work that person does in one hour, week or month (behaviour), they will be  paid the same amount (reinforcement). In operant conditioning, a fixed-interval schedule is a  simple reinforcement schedule in which reward follows the first response that the organism  makes after a predetermined time interval, and then the first response that it makes after the  same interval, and so on.

questions.question_text: Dr. Lepage is a GP who gets extra payments for every additional hour of clinical work that he undertakes. This reinforcement schedule is an example of
questions.explanation: With a fixed-ratio schedule, there are a set number of responses that must occur before the  behaviour is rewarded. In this example, the doctor earns extra money for every extra hour of  clinic he does (interval is fixed). Fixed ratios are better suited to optimize the quantity of  output, whereas a fixed interval can lead to a higher quality of output. In operant conditioning,  a fixed-interval schedule is a simple reinforcement schedule in which reward follows the first  response that the organism makes after a predetermined time interval, and then the first  response that it makes after the same interval, and so on.

questions.question_text: After a consultation with a GP, one of your patients was able to recall verbatim the opening statement asked by the GP. This is described as
questions.explanation: The primacy effect describes the tendency to remember items presented at the beginning of a list better than those presented later. The correct answer is: Primacy effect.

questions.question_text: The Tarasoff case was related to
questions.explanation: The Tarasoff case set a precedent for the duty to warn third parties regarding potential dangers posed by a patient's violent intentions, impacting confidentiality practices. The correct answer is: Confidentiality.

questions.question_text: The double-bind theory in schizophrenia refers to

options.text: Migration being a precipitant for psychosis
Lack of motivation to remain abstinent from cocaine use
Giving contradictory messages to a child
One parent assumes a dominant and the other a submissive role
Parents downgrading the roles of each other

correct_answer.text: Giving contradictory messages to a child

correct_answers.text: Giving contradictory messages to a child

questions.explanation: Gregory Bateson and Donald Jackson formulated the double bind concept. It was used to  describe a hypothetical family, in which children receive conflicting parental messages about  their behaviour, attitude and feelings. According to Bateson's hypothesis, children withdraw  into a psychotic state to escape the unsolvable confusion of the double bind.
